title.label: Messes with Markdown where it didn’t used to.

content.label:
*Sigh*

There comes a time in every app’s life when the pressure to reach more people, an itch to make long desired changes, or simple developer boredom necessitates wholesale changes to a beloved, award-winning app. Sometimes these changes are welcome, sometimes they’re tolerated, most of the time, we grumble for a week, get used to them, and continue on. Too often we move on to something else and mourn the loss of our favorite app, entirely. 

Today is that day. Which of these scenarios will play out is yet to know, but I hope enough of my peers agree with some of my initial complaints and the developers listen and offer up changes to provide a fifth path forward: minor tweaks and improvements to allow those who would otherwise leave, to stay. 

So let’s talk Markdown. Those of us who have loved it most and use it every day (I’m writing a dissertation in Markdown) typically don’t want anything but Markdown. These days, live markup combined with the Markdown syntax is a welcome addition to legibility, scan ability, and is fairly easy to support. That means **bold** is both bold and includes two little asterisks on either side. For _years_, Bear did this so well. Almost better than anyone else (iA Writer had the en beat by a pinch, though). Their only issues were nested styles (bold _and_ italic, say) and some odd decisions about Themes, colors, and indenting that were more than acceptable. Bullets had a negative padding and some syntax was replaced with red (by default) and stylized syntax instead of the native * or - or whatever.

Bear 2.0 actually fixes some of these styling issues, like negative padding. In some cases, that changes how some of my existing notes read, but because I wrote them with a flawed system in the first place and we are now in a better place, that’s on me. 

In other ways, though, Bear 2.0 goes out of its way to be more complicated, less Markdown native, and, I suppose, maybe a bit more friendly to folks who don’t like or use Markdown for its native legibility. Good for those cases, I suppose. Bullets how have multiple levels:

- Red dot, filled
  - Red dot, empty 
    - Red diamond, filled
      - Red diamond, empty
        - Back to red dot, filled

They also offer the option of showing or hiding Markdown syntax (Hide is the default, which should probably tell me who their largest customer base is), but it’s when that option is checked, that the bigger issue emerges. 

Disabling Hide Markdown doesn’t actually leave (all) Markdown. One of the most oft-used and easy-to-read Markdown syntax structures is the # Heading. Bear replaces easy-to-read # with a bizarre glyph of a set of lines forming a paragraph and a Heading number (1 through n) in the bottom right. Not only is the spacing and legibility of the # lost in favor of a bizarre glyph and tiny number (strangely at the bottom of the paragraph, not the top), but when using the Delete key, it is impossible to edit the number of # without deleting all and retyping, or tapping the glyph and choosing the new Heading level. The Markdown is basically gone at this point, replaced with a Bear system that is only _created_ with Markdown, not Markdown, itself. This is particularly strange, because in normal text, the syntax is left alone and you can delete syntax at the end of a string without it destroying the matching syntax at the beginning, a scenario that would actually, kind of benefit from some programmatic smarts. 

So, what am I really saying? I guess I’m asking that Markdown be Markdown and Bear be Bear. If there is going to remain an option for writing and leaving Markdown in the app, just be cool with leaving it in its entirety, not picking and choosing bits and pieces. At a moment when Apple’s own system apps are starting ti embrace Markdown syntax, why would Bear move away from it, even when they they recognize that some people still want it?

There are so many other things in this update to love: custom fonts, sections, and the new keyboard (though I wish I could customize an alway-present bar of three or so things to allow things that can’t be typed out on an iOS keyboard, like Tab (now three taps instead of one). I could complain about the Export and Copy-as menu, but Apple is enabling and developers are jumping in the sub-menu train and I’m not you going to chase after it. Plain Text _is_ Markdown, but I get what you’re doing and can adjust my expectations. I’d also like adjustable spacing in the Notes list (I think everything got a little more room), but, I’m ok with those most little things. 

Just don’t mess with my Markdown.

title.label: Simply the best notes app for iPadOS

content.label:
UPDATE: Bear 2

Everything from my original review applies except that all the features that Bear 1 was missing have now been integrated with the release of Bear 2. This is the best notes, knowledge management, journaling, and writing app, hands down.

——

Original: I’ve tried them all on iPad: Obsidian, Craft, Notion, Ulysses, Notes, Notion, etc. Nothing compares with Bear. It may be lacking in some certain powerful features (back links and tables, being the primary ones, though they’re coming in v2.x). But I need my notes app to first and foremost work, and work smoothly. I need it to get out of the way when I want to create new notes and find existing notes. Bear is lightweight and efficient, even with thousands of interlinked notes. Looking forward to many more years of Bear!

If you’re looking for a first-class notes app that embraces Markdown and works on all of your Apple devices, you should give Bear a shot. I’ve been a paying user for years and the app has only gotten better in that time.

title.label: Great note taking app with one fatal flaw

However it lacks one essential feature that even Notes has: collaboration and sharing notes with other people, that prevents it from being a must have.

title.label: Version 2.0 adds all the missing pieces 👍🏻

content.label:
I’ve been using Bear for years, and have a Pro subscription to add syncing between devices. I love it’s simple but useful UI and use of markdown, and I enjoy the light-hearted nature of the app presentation / identity.

For a long time there has been minor but noticeable missing functionality, such as back-links and searching within notes. For this reason I’ve occasionally tried other apps such as Notion, OneNote, and Craft, but they either had a UI design paradigm that didn’t click with me, and/or were much more expensive subscriptions.

As of version 2.0 Bear has added all of the functions I’ve been missing, plus a ton more. I now have no reservations about whole-heartedly recommending it above any other note-taking app. 👍🏻 Great work, Bear team!
